pages.x: Hong Xiuquan, a village teacher from near Canton, failed the imperial exams four times. After one failure he fell ill and saw visions, and years later, reading a Christian pamphlet, he decided they meant that he was the younger brother of Jesus, sent to rid China of demons: by which he came to mean its Manchu rulers.

His God Worshipping Society drew in poor miners, farmers and Hakka people in Guangxi province. In 1851 Hong declared the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace, Taiping Tianguo. His followers grew their hair long, refusing the shaved forehead and braid the Manchus forced on men, and banned opium, gambling, alcohol and the binding of girls' feet.

The Taiping swept north into the Yangtze valley, and in March 1853 they took Nanjing, the old southern capital, and killed its Manchu people. Hong renamed it Tianjing, the Heavenly Capital, and ruled from a palace there for eleven years. An army he sent north to take Beijing got close to Tianjin before it was destroyed.

In Taiping lands men and women lived apart, even husbands and wives, and women served as soldiers and officials. Land was to be shared out equally and goods held in common. But Hong withdrew into his palace, and in 1856 his leaders turned on each other: one of them, the East King, was killed with thousands of his followers.

The Qing's own armies were rotten, so a Confucian scholar from Hunan, Zeng Guofan, raised a new one from his home province, paid for by local taxes and loyal to its own officers. His Xiang Army fought its way down the Yangtze year by year, winning back city after city.

The Western powers, at first curious about Chinese Christians, decided they would rather have a weak Qing that kept its treaties. Around Shanghai a force of Chinese soldiers with foreign officers, the Ever-Victorious Army, fought for the Qing, led from 1863 by a British officer, Charles Gordon, later known as Chinese Gordon.

In June 1864 Hong died, ill, as Zeng's armies closed in. In July they broke into Nanjing and killed perhaps 100,000 people there. The fighting dragged on for years more, and whole districts of the Yangtze valley were left empty. It was the deadliest civil war in history.
pages.of: people died, most of hunger and disease

pages.x: The Qing survived, but weaker, and leaning on regional armies like Zeng's whose generals became the warlords of the next century. Sun Yat-sen, who overthrew the dynasty in 1911, grew up on tales of the Taiping and called himself a second Hong Xiuquan, and China's Communists praised them as early revolutionaries.
